title: A Group-Theoretical Framework for Local k-Space Topology and Berry Phase in 2D Photonic Systems
abstract: Two-dimensional photonic crystals (2D PhCs) enable fine-grained control over a broad set of Bloch modes without the constraints of band occupancy and natural crystal structures, and, as intrinsically open systems, serve as versatile platforms for exploring diverse topological phenomena. Here, we develop a theoretical framework inspired by the irreducible-representation formalism in solid-state physics, while explicitly incorporating key characteristics of photonic Bloch systems, such as radiative coupling and transverse condition. Within this framework, we study the symmetry origins of local k-space topology, e.g., bound-states in the continuum and optical vortex beams, and Berry phase in two representative systems. We further analyze, from a group-theory perspective, how tailored structural designs and targeted symmetry perturbations can be exploited to manipulate these topological features. In particular, we showcase the application of the formalism to Bloch modes from distinct truncation approaches and specify the preferable regimes for each, both under a generic $n$-band configuration. The analysis can thereby be readily extended to a wide range of artificial wave crystals beyond scalar Schrödinger-like operators and two-level treatment.
summary: The paper establishes a group-theoretical framework to analyze topological properties like Berry phase and BICs in 2D Photonic Crystals. By adapting solid-state IR formalism, it systematically maps how crystal symmetries dictate mode behavior. This provides a powerful tool for designing photonic structures with tailored topological responses.
main_problem: To develop a group-theoretical framework for understanding local k-space topology and Berry phase in 2D Photonic Crystals (PhCs).
main_result: The irreducible-representation formalism allows for the systematic classification of topological phenomena, showing that non-Abelian groups are key for Berry phase emergence.
method: Applying group theory concepts, specifically decomposing basis functions using symmetry operations and block-diagonalizing the Bloch Hamiltonian to analyze mode coupling.
model_or_system: The system is 2D Photonic Crystals (PhCs), modeled by a Bloch Hamiltonian adapted from solid-state physics, incorporating radiative coupling and transverse conditions. The analysis extends beyond scalar Schrödinger operators.
key_observables: Local k-space topology, Berry phase, symmetry-protected degeneracies, BIC linewidths, and mode hybridization conditions.
important_parameters: High symmetry points ($\Gamma$-point), structural design parameters, and coefficients associated with targeted irreducible representations (IRs).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system can be effectively decoupled from the radiation continuum for initial block decomposition, though extensions are discussed.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows representative site geometries in real space for square and triangular lattices, annotated with little groups at high-symmetry points.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the IR formalism to classify topology, applies it to study BICs/vortex beams using PWE and non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, and concludes by detailing how structural or gain/loss perturbations can systematically manipulate these topological features.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful mathematical tool (group theory) to analyze wave phenomena in engineered optical structures, bridging solid-state topology concepts directly into the realm of photonics and open quantum systems.
